pages.sourceText:
PSYCH 301  ·  Ch. 5  Short-Term Memory
What Is Memory?
MEMORY BASICS
●Memory: processes involved in retaining, 
retrieving, and using information about 
stimuli, images, events, ideas, and skills after 
the original information is no longer present
●Active any time some past experience has an 
impact on how you think or behave now or in 
the future
–
Memory has to do with the past affecting the 
present, and possibly the future
Endel Tulving (not shown here) describes episodic memory as a kind of “mental 
time travel.”
http://www.apa.org/monitor/oct03/mental.aspx

pages.title: Encoding, storage, and retrieval
pages.sourceText:
PSYCH 301  ·  Ch. 5  Short-Term Memory
Memory: Key Terms
MEMORY BASICS
Memory: Active system that stores, organizes, alters, 
and recovers (retrieves) information
Encoding: Converting information into a useable form 
for storage
Storage: Holding this information in memory
Retrieval: Taking memories out of storage
Computer scientists had to think a lot harder about short-term vs. long-
term memory when RAM maxed out at 16KB.

pages.title: Large capacity and fast decay
pages.sourceText:
PSYCH 301  ·  Ch. 5  Short-Term Memory
Sperling (1960): Iconic Memory
SENSORY MEMORY
What’s the point?
●Sperling was studying visual sensory memory
●Before his study, people thought that visual sensory memory could only hold 4-5 items (full report 
cond)
●The other conditions in his study showed that
–
It’s true that people can only report 4-5 items before memory decays (or fades away)
–
BUT sensory memory actually encodes the whole scene
Conclusion: Sensory Memory has a large capacity, but fast decay
Within just 1 second, most of sensory memory decays, leaving only what was moved to STM via attention.

●It turns out, their studies demonstrate that another type of forgetting that happens in STM: proactive

pages.title: Working memory stores and manipulates information
pages.sourceText:
Working Memory
• Modal model view of STM turned out to be too simple
– STM is not just passive storage, but also requires “control 
processes,” so we need a model that includes those 
somehow…
• Baddeley and Hitch (1974): Working memory - Similar 
concept to short-term memory
• Working memory: limited capacity system for temporary 
storage and manipulation of information for complex tasks 
such as comprehension, learning, and reasoning

pages.title: Mental multiplication combines storage with processing
pages.sourceText:
Working Memory
• “multiply 43 times 6 in your head”
1. Visualize: 43 * 6
2. Multiply 3 * 6 = 18
3. Hold 8 in memory, while carrying the 1 over the 4
4. Multiply 6 * 4 = 24, then add the carried 1 = 25
5. Combine 25 and the 8 you were holding = 258
This operation involves both storage (holding 8 in memory) & active 
processes (carrying the 1…)

pages.title: Short-term memory and working-memory models
pages.sourceText:
Comparing Memory Models
• Short-term Memory (Atkinson & Shiffrin)
– Single component for all types of info
– Mainly used for holding information for a short time
• Working Memory (Baddeley & Hitch)
– Three components:
• Central Executive
• Visuospatial Sketchpad
• Phonological Loop
• (+ Episodic Buffer, added by Baddeley in 2000)
– Used for manipulation of information during complex cognition

pages.title: The loop, sketchpad, and executive have different jobs
pages.sourceText:
Components of Working Memory
• Phonological Loop
– Phonological store: Holds verbal and auditory information
– Articulatory rehearsal process: responsible for rehearsal that can keep items in the 
phonological store from decaying
• Visuospatial Sketch Pad
– Holds visual and spatial information
• Central Executive
– Pulls info from long-term memory, coordinates other components, directs and maintains 
attention…

pages.title: Working-memory components interact with long-term knowledge
pages.sourceText:
Working Memory
Baddeley & Hitch (1974)

pages.title: Three effects associated with the phonological loop
pages.sourceText:
Phonological Loop
• Phonological similarity effect
– Letters or words that sound similar are confused
• Word-length effect
– Memory for lists of words is better for short words than for long words
– Takes longer to rehearse long words and to produce them during recall
• Articulatory suppression
– Speaking interferes with rehearsal, therefore memory is reduced

pages.title: Conrad’s flashed letters are confused by sound
pages.sourceText:
Phonological Similarity Effect
• The basic effect: words that sound similar are confused by people
• Conrad (1964)
– Participants saw target letters (quickly flashed)
– Half of the time the letters were similar and half of the time they weren’t
– Then they wrote them down
– Mistakes were made
• Not likely to replace with something that looked like the target (E for F)
• Likely to replace with something that SOUNDED like the target (E for B)

pages.title: Visual letters can be recoded into sound
pages.sourceText:
Phonological Similarity Effect
• The Phonological Similarity Effect experiment:
– Demonstrated the phonological similarity effect (people confuse letters that 
sound similar)
• even though information was presented visually
– As we’ll see later, it also showed that the phonological loop is necessary for the 
conversion (not just holding info)

pages.title: Word length changes how much can be rehearsed
pages.sourceText:
Word-Length Effect
• The basic effect: When memorizing words, you can remember fewer words if the 
words are long
– People remembered more of the short words than long words (Baddeley et al., 
1975, 1984)
– Welsh–English bilingual children have a shorter digit span in Welsh than in English 
(Ellis & Hennelly, 1980)
• Because Welsh numbers take longer to pronounce!
– The number of words you can say in 1.5-2.0 seconds is likely to be your digit span

pages.title: Articulatory suppression disrupts verbal rehearsal
pages.sourceText:
Articulatory Suppression
• The basic finding: if you speak while memorizing (which keeps the phonological loop 
busy):
– you get worse at remembering,
– the word length and phonological similarity effects are reduced
• What is going on in these situations? Why does this support the concept of a 
phonological loop?

pages.title: The visuospatial sketchpad supports mental imagery
pages.sourceText:
Visuospatial Sketch Pad
• The visuospatial sketch pad holds visual and spatial information
• Involved in the process of visual imagery

pages.title: Brooks’s sentence task is easier with pointing
pages.sourceText:
Visuospatial Sketch Pad
• Brooks (1968) – the sentence experiment
– Memorize a sentence
– Indicate whether each word is / is not a noun
• Condition 1: indicate by speaking
• Condition 2: indicate by pointing
– Results: pointing was easier than speaking for the participants
• Explanation: Phonological loop was busy processing the sentence, but sketch pad 
was free

pages.title: Brooks’s F task is easier with speaking
pages.sourceText:
Visuospatial Sketch Pad
• Brooks (1968) – the “F” demo
– Memorize a shape (in this case an F)
– Indicate whether each corner is an “inside corner” 
or an “outside corner”
• Condition 1: Indicate by speaking
• Condition 2: Indicate by pointing
– Results: Speaking is easier than pointing (the 
OPPOSITE of what happened before)
• Explanation: Sketch Pad was busy with image, but 
phonological loop was free

pages.title: Interference depends on the combination of tasks
pages.sourceText:
Visuospatial Sketch Pad
• Tasks are easier when the information being held in mind and the operation being 
performed on it involve different types of short-term memory
– Verbal / Phonological
– Visual / Spatial
• That means that the two types of short-term memory are somewhat independent
– At the least, separate capacities

pages.title: Executive control directs the work of working memory
pages.sourceText:
The Central Executive
• The Central Executive does the “work” of working 
memory
– Directing and maintaining attention
• Focus, divide, switch attention
– Controls suppression of irrelevant information
– Coordinating sketchpad and phonological loop
– Performing calculations
– Today often split into updating, shifting, and 
inhibition (Miyake et al., 2000)
The idea of a “central executive” is 
often criticized as theorizing a 
“homunculus” in the brain.

pages.title: The episodic buffer binds information into episodes
pages.sourceText:
The Episodic Buffer (Baddeley, 2000)
• A fourth component, added to the model in 2000
– Limited capacity (about 4 “chunks”)
– Binds information from the loop, sketch pad, and long-term memory into integrated 
“episodes”
• Why was it needed?
– People can recall ~16 words of a meaningful sentence, far beyond span for unrelated words
– Some amnesic patients can immediately recall a just-heard story

pages.title: Gestalt representation and restructuring in Köhler’s circle problem
pages.sourceText:
Gestalt Approach
•
Gestalt psychologists were interested not only in perception but also in 
learning, problem solving, and even attitudes and beliefs (Koffka, 1935)
–
They took a perceptual approach to dealing with all the above 
•
Problem solving for Gestalt psychologists was about:
– Representing a problem in the mind
– Restructuring: reorganization or restructuring the problem’s representation
• Kohler’s “circle” problem
•
Different people might 
represent this problem 
differently
•
People’s representations is 
likely to be different from the 
picture on this slide
•
If the length of the circle’s 
radius is r, what is the 
length of line x?

pages.title: Insight is a sudden realization after restructuring
pages.sourceText:
Insight in Problem-Solving
•
Often solutions are obtained by first perceiving the object and then 
representing it in a different way
–
➔ restructuring of the problem’s representation
•
Gestalt psychologists related restructuring with insight
– Sudden realization of a problem’s solution
– Discovering a crucial element 
– They thought solutions come to people all of a sudden
– “Aha” experience
•
Other researchers don’t necessarily agree with this
– A lot of our problem solving does not require “Aha” experiences

pages.title: Metcalfe and Wiebe measured perceived closeness to a solution
pages.sourceText:
Insight in Problem-Solving
•
Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987): designed an experiment to distinguish 
between insight and noninsight problems
– Insight: triangle problem, chain problem
– Noninsight: algebra
– Hypothesis: 
• In insight problems: S should not be very good at predicting how near they 
are to a solution
• In non-insight problems: involves more methodical process ➔ S should know 
how close they are to the solution
– Warmth judgments every 15 seconds: “hot” ratings indicated that 
they are getting close to the problem

pages.title: Triangle and chain problems require a change in representation
pages.sourceText:
Insight in Problem-Solving
Show how you can move three of the 
blue dots to get the triangle to point to 
the bottom of the page
Join the pieces on the left into a single 
closed loop of chain (as on the right). To 
open a link costs 2 cents and to close a 
link costs 3 cents. You only have 15 
cents…

pages.title: Warmth rises gradually for algebra and suddenly for insight
pages.sourceText:
Insight in Problem-Solving
•
Metcalfe and Wiebe (1987) “warmer/colder” rating
– Insight problems solved suddenly
– Noninsight problems solved gradually
Big jump from 3 to 7
Gradual increase

pages.title: Functional fixedness in the candle problem
pages.sourceText:
Obstacles to Problem-Solving
•
Gestalt psychologists claimed that one of the major obstacles to 
problem solving is fixation
–
Tendency to focus on a specific characteristic of the problem that keeps people 
from arriving at a solution
•
Functional fixedness: restricting use of an object to its familiar 
functions
Candle problem: You are in a room with a  
vertical corkboard mounted on the wall. You 
are given the material on the right. Mount a 
candle on the corkboard so it will burn 
without dripping was on the floor
Seeing matchboxes as containers inhibited using them as supports
•
S who were given empty matchboxes instead, were twice as likely to solve 
the problem

pages.title: Pliers can serve as a weight in the two-string problem
pages.sourceText:
Obstacles to Problem-Solving
•
Gestalt psychologists claimed that one of the major obstacles to 
problem solving is fixation
–
Tendency to focus on a specific characteristic of the problem that keeps people 
from arriving at a solution
•
Functional fixedness: restricting use of an object to its familiar 
functions
Two-string problem: Tie together the two 
strings
function of pliers gets in the way of seeing them 
as a weight
They can be used to create a pendulum

pages.title: A swinging-string hint and a mental set affect representation
pages.sourceText:
Obstacles to Problem-Solving
•
Two string problem: once a hint was provided by “accidentally” 
setting the string in motion, most of the S were able to solve it
–
In Gestalt terms: the solution occurred when S restructures their representation
•
Mental set
– A preconceived notion about how to approach a problem
– Based on a person’s past experiences with the problem (or 
similar problems)
– Water-jug problem: figure out how to obtain a required volume of 
water, given three empty jars for measure

pages.title: Water-jug experience can hide a simpler solution
pages.sourceText:
Each problem specifies the 
capacities of jugs A, B, and C and a 
final desired quantity. 
The task is to figure out how to use 
the jugs with these capacities to 
measure out the desired quantity. 
Obstacles to Problem-Solving
Given mental set inhibited participants 
from using simpler solution

pages.title: Newell and Simon treated solving as search through a problem space
pages.sourceText:
Information-Processing Approach
•
Newell and Simon (1956): Logic theorist
•
Described problem solving as a process that involves search
–
Instead of just considering the initial structure and then the new structure 
achieved when the problem is solved
•
➔ Newell and Simon described problem solving as a search that 
occurs between the posing of the problem and its solution
–
“searching for a way to reach a goal”
–
“getting around road-blocks”
•
Problem space
– Initial state: conditions at the beginning of the problem
– Intermediate state(s)
– Goal state: solution of the problem

pages.title: Operators define legal moves in the Tower of Hanoi
pages.sourceText:
Information-Processing Approach
•
Operators: rules specify which moves are allowed and which are not
–
Take the state of the problem from one state to another
•
Tower of Hanoi
•
Disks are used one at a 
time
•
A disk can be moved only 
when there are no discs on 
top of it
•
A larger disk cannot be 
placed on top of a smaller 
disk

pages.title: Tower of Hanoi requires repeated intermediate rearrangements
pages.sourceText:
Information-Processing Approach
With 64 disks, it will 
take a trillion years to 
solve it, even if each 
moved was made in a 
second, and it was 
correct

pages.title: Numbered-tile arrangements define the start and goal
pages.sourceText: Information-Processing Approach

pages.title: A search tree connects alternative tile-puzzle states
pages.sourceText: Information-Processing Approach

pages.title: Means–end analysis uses subgoals to reduce a difference
pages.sourceText:
Information-Processing Approach
•
According to Newell and Simon, we have to search the problem space 
to find a solution
•
Means-end analysis: reduce differences between initial and goal 
states
– Subgoals: create intermediate states closer to goal
•
For Tower of Hanoi, applying means-end analysis reduces the size of 
the difference between initial and goal states

pages.title: Tower of Hanoi subgoals free the large disk and the target peg
pages.sourceText: Information-Processing Approach

pages.title: How a problem is stated can change its difficulty
pages.sourceText:
The Importance of How a Problem Is Stated
•
One of the main contributions of Newell and Simon’s approach: 
provided a way to specify the possible pathways from the initial to 
goal states
•
There is more to problem solving than specifying the problem state 
•
How a problem is stated can affect its difficulty
•
Mutilated-checkerboard problem

pages.title: Opposite removed corners make a domino covering impossible
pages.sourceText:
The Importance of How a Problem Is Stated
Checkerboard: 64 squares, can be 
completely covered by placing 32 
dominos on the board so that each 
domino covers 2 squares
Mutilated checkerboard 
problem:
If we eliminate 2 corners, can 
we now cover the remaining 
squares with 31 dominos?

pages.title: Bread-and-butter labels make the pairing constraint available
pages.sourceText:
The Importance of How a Problem Is Stated
•
Mutilated-checkerboard problem
– Key to solving it: understanding that
1. Each domino covers two squares
2. These squares must be of different colors
– Conditions differed in how much information provided about the squares
1. Blank board
2. Colored board
3. Words black and pink on the board
4. Words bread and butter on the board
– Easier to solve when information is provided that points toward the 
correct representation of the problem
• “Bread and butter” condition emphasized the difference between the squares
• S solved this condition twice as fast as the blank condition

pages.title: Think-aloud protocols record thoughts during solving
pages.sourceText:
The Importance of How a Problem Is Stated
•
Think-aloud protocol
– Say aloud what one is thinking when solving a problem
• Instructed not to describe what you are doing, but verbalize new 
thoughts
• Goal: what information S is attending to while solving the problem
– Shift in how one perceives elements of a problem
• S get the problem after realizing that the word “bread” and “butter” 
are important
• Similar to the gestalt idea of representational shift

pages.title: Problem Solving and Reasoning · Part II · title
pages.sourceText:
PSYCH 301 
Cognitive Processes
Lecture 14:
Problem-Solving and Reasoning
Fall 2026
Instructor: Bryan Shilowich

pages.title: Problem solving involves representation, search, and how the task is stated
pages.sourceText:
Problem solving
•
Problem solving as reorganization and insight
•
Problem solving as search: a search that occurs between the posing of the 
problem and its solution
•
There is more to problem solving than specifying the problem state 
•
How a problem is stated can affect its difficulty

pages.title: The Russian marriage problem depends on equal numbers of two groups
pages.sourceText:
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem
•
Using a solution to a similar problem guides solution to new problem
– In a small Russian village, there were 32 bachelors and 32 
unmarried women. Through tireless efforts, the village 
matchmaker succeeded in arranging 32 highly satisfactory 
marriages. The village was proud and happy. Then one drunken 
night, two bachelors, in a test of strength, stuffed each other with 
pierogies and died. Can the matchmaker, through some quick 
arrangements, come up with 31 heterosexual marriages among 
the 62 survivors?

pages.title: Opposite missing corners leave an imbalance between square colors
pages.sourceText: Using Analogies to Solve a Problem

pages.title: Analogical transfer maps a source problem onto a target problem
pages.sourceText:
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem
•
Analogical problem solving: Using a solution to a similar problem 
guides solution to new problem
– Russian marriage problem (source problem) → mutilated-
checkerboard problem (target problem)
– Analogical transfer: The transfer from one problem to another
• Source problem to target problem
– Target problem: the problem that S is trying to solve
– Source problem:  another problem that shares some similarities with the 
target problem
• Learning about the Russian marriage problem enhances the 
ability to solve the mutilated-checkerboard problem

pages.title: Duncker’s radiation problem requires a strong effect without damaging the path
pages.sourceText:
•
Duncker’s radiation problem:
– Try solving the following problem:
– Suppose you are a doctor faced with a patient who has a malignant tumor in 
his stomach. It is impossible to operate on the patient, but unless the tumor is 
destroyed the patient will die. There is a kind of ray that can be used to 
destroy the tumor. If the rays reach it all at once at a sufficiently high intensity, 
the tumor will be destroyed. Unfortunately, at this intensity the healthy tissue 
the rays pass through on the way to the tumor will also be destroyed. At lower 
intensities the rays are harmless to healthy tissue, but they will not affect the 
tumor, either. What type of procedure might be used to destroy the tumor 
with the rays and at the same time avoid destroying the healthy tissue?
•
Only 10% of S arrive at the correct solution
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem

pages.title: The fortress problem separates safe routes from the force needed at the target
pages.sourceText:
•
A small country was ruled from a strong fortress by a dictator. The fortress was 
situated in the middle of the country, surrounded by farms and villages. Many 
roads led to the fortress through the countryside. A rebel general vowed to 
capture the fortress. The general knew that an attack by his entire army would 
capture the fortress. He gathered his army at the head of one of the roads, ready 
to launch a full-scale direct attack. However, the general then learned that the 
dictator had planted mines on each of the roads. The mines were set so that small 
bodies of men could pass over them safely, since the dictator needed to move his 
troops and workers to and from the fortress. However, any large force would 
detonate the mines. Not only would this blow up the road, but it would also 
destroy many neighboring villages. It therefore seemed impossible to capture the 
fortress.
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem

pages.title: Small attacking groups correspond to converging low-intensity rays
pages.sourceText: Using Analogies to Solve a Problem

pages.title: Noticing, mapping, and applying an analogy are separate steps
pages.sourceText:
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem
•
After reading the fortress story, 30% of S arrive at the correct solution
•
Gick and Holyoak
– Noticing an analogous relationship
• Crucial, and the most difficult step
– Mapping correspondence between source and target
• Elements of the source need to be mapped to element of the target
– Applying mapping
• to generate parallel solutions in target
•
70% of S where not able to see the correspondences 
–
When S were told to think about the story they had read, success rate got to 75%

pages.title: Surface features can hide a shared relationship
pages.sourceText:
•
There are factors that facilitate the noticing and mapping steps 
•
One reason noticing is difficult is that people often focus on surface 
features
–
Fortress and tumor 
•
Can making surface features similar facilitate noticing analogous 
relationships? 
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem

pages.title: The lightbulb problem preserves a target-and-surroundings constraint
pages.sourceText:
•
In a physics lab at a major university, a very expensive lightbulb, which would emit 
precisely controlled quantities of light, was being used in some experiments. One 
morning Ruth, the research assistant, came into the lab and found that lightbulb 
no longer worked. She noticed that the filament inside the bulb had broken into 
two parts. The surrounding glass bulb was completely sealed, so there was no way 
to open it. Ruth knew that the lightbuild could be repaired if a brief, high intensity 
laser beam could be used to fuse the two parts of the filament into one.
•
However, a high-intensity laser beam would also break the fragile glass 
surrounding the filament. At lower intensities the laser would not break the glass, 
but neither would it fuse the filament. What type of procedure might be used to 
fuse the filament with the laser and at the same time avoid breaking the glass?
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem

pages.title: A radiation source improves transfer to the lightbulb target
pages.sourceText:
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem
•
Duncker’s Radiation Problem used as the source
– 81% of S that knew about the radiation problem solved the 
lightbulb problem 
– 10% of S in the control group were able to solve the problem
•
Surface similarity helped in solving the problem

pages.title: Surface features name objects, while structural features govern the solution
pages.sourceText:
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem
•
Lightbulb problem
– High surface similarities aid analogical problem solving
• Surface features: Specific elements of a given problem
– What about structural features?
• Underlying principle that governs the solution
– Radiation: strong ray destroys tissue
– Lightbulb: strong laser breaks lightbulb
• Made two versions, keeping the surface features the same and varying the 
structural features

pages.title: Fragile glass supplies the same structural obstacle as vulnerable tissue
pages.sourceText:
•
Source problem 1: Fragile-Glass version (source and target have similar 
structural features)
•
Problem: A high-intensity laser beam would break the fragile glass 
surrounding the filament. At lower intensities the laser would not break 
the glass, but neither would it fuse the filament.
•
Ruth’s Solution: Ruth placed several lasers in a circle around the lightbulb 
and administered low-intensity laser beams from several directions at 
once. The beams all converged on the filament, where their combined 
effect was enough to fuse it. Because each spot on the surrounding glass 
received only a low-intensity beak from each laser, the glass was left 
intact.
•
69% of S who read this solution were able to solve the radiation problem
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem

pages.title: Insufficient laser intensity changes the source’s structural features
pages.sourceText:
•
Source problem 2: Insufficient-Intensity version (source and target have 
different structural features)
•
Problem: The laser generated only low-intensity beams that were not 
strong enough to fuse the filament. A much more intense laser beam was 
needed.
•
Ruth’s Solution: Ruth placed several lasers in a circle around the lightbulb 
and administered low-intensity laser beams from several directions at 
once. The beam all converged on the filament, where their combined 
effect was enough to fuse it.
•
33% of S who read this solution were able to solve the radiation problem
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem

pages.title: Analogical encoding compares problems to identify structural similarities
pages.sourceText:
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem
•
Making structural features more obvious aids analogical problem-
solving
• Structural features: The underlying principle(s) that govern 
the solution to a problem
•
Analogical encoding: the process by which two problems are 
compared and similarities between them are determined
– Effective way to get participants to pay attention to structural 
features that aide problem-solving
– Having people compare source stories may be an effective way to 
force S focus on structural features

pages.title: Analogies can be difficult to transfer in a lab and common in everyday work
pages.sourceText:
Using Analogies to Solve a Problem
•
Analogical paradox
– It can be difficult to apply analogies in the laboratory, but people 
routinely use analogies in real-world settings
– Scientists use about 3 to 15 analogies in a 1-hour lab meeting
•
In vivo problem-solving research
– People are observed to determine how they solve problems in the 
real world
• Advantage: naturalistic setting
• Disadvantages: time-consuming, cannot isolate and control 
variables

pages.title: Expertise develops through learning, practice, and application in a field
pages.sourceText:
How Experts Solve Problems
•
What is an expert?
– “A person who, by devoting a large amount of time to learning 
about a field and practicing and applying that learning, have  
become acknowledged as being extremely knowledgeable or 
skilled in that field.”
• Chess expert: someone who has spent 10,000 to 20,000 hours studying and 
playing chess
•
Experts solve problems in their field faster and with a higher success 
rate than beginners
•
But why are they better?

pages.title: Chase and Simon linked chess recall to familiar, meaningful chunks
pages.sourceText:
•
Experts possess more knowledge about their fields
•
Chase & Simon (1973): compared how well a chess master and a beginner 
(fewer than 100 hours)  were able to reproduce the positions of pieces on 
a chessboard after looking at an arrangement for 5 seconds
•
Two conditions:
–
Pieces arranged in actual game positions
–
Pieces arranged randomly 
•
Experts did much better than non-experts in the first condition
–
They had stored these actual position in their LTM
–
The positions were accessed in chunks
–
These chunks were not available in the random condition
How Experts Solve Problems

pages.title: Chi and colleagues compared how experts and novices group physics problems
pages.sourceText:
How Experts Solve Problems
•
Knowledge is organized so it can be accessed when needed to work 
on a problem
•
Chi et al. (1982): presented 24 physics problems to a group of experts 
(physics professors) and a group of novices (students with one 
semester of physics) 
– They were asked to sort the problems into groups based on their 
similarities 
– Novices: sorted based on surface features (what the object looked 
like)
– Experts: sorted based on structural features (the underlying 
principles involved)

pages.title: Inclined planes can look alike while an expert groups by conservation of energy
pages.sourceText: How Experts Solve Problems

pages.title: Expert analysis helps within a field but familiar procedures can restrict flexibility
pages.sourceText:
How Experts Solve Problems
•
Experts spend more time analyzing problem
–
Slower start, but this strategy usually pays off
•
Experts are no better than novices when given problems outside of 
their field
•
Being an expert is not always an advantage
•
Experts less likely to be open to new ways of looking at problems
–
Being an expert may be a disadvantage when confronting a problem that requires 
flexible thinking
• Problems whose solution may involve rejecting the usual procedures in favor 
of other procedures that are less frequently used

pages.title: Creative problem solving includes generating, evaluating, and implementing ideas
pages.sourceText:
Creative Problem-Solving
•
Creativity
– Innovative thinking
– Novel ideas
– New connections between existing ideas
– Divergent thinking: open-ended; large number of potential 
“solutions”
•
Problem solving as a process: most creative problem solving includes 
far more than just getting an idea
–
It involves a lengthy period of trial-and-error
–
Stages:
• Problem generation: Problem finding, fact finding
• Problem formulation: Problem definition, idea finding
• Problem solving: Evaluation, planning
• Solution implementation: taking action

pages.title: Ideas are necessary, and flexible thinking can require rejecting familiar procedures
pages.sourceText:
Creative Problem-Solving
•
Generating ideas is only one part of the creative process
–
Without ideas, the process stops
•
Too much knowledge can sometimes hinder creative problem solving
–
Often problems require thinking flexibility and rejecting accepted procedures

pages.title: Judgment, Decision Making, and Reasoning · title
pages.sourceText:
PSYCH 301CL
Cognitive Processes
Fall 2026
Bryan Shilowich
Lecture 15: 
Judgment, Decision Making, and
Reasoning

pages.title: Decisions choose between alternatives, while reasoning draws conclusions
pages.sourceText:
Decisions and Reasoning
•
Decisions: The process of making choices between alternatives
•
Reasoning: The process of drawing conclusions
•
Decisions are based on judgments we make, and applying these 
judgments can involve various reasoning processes
•
One of the primary mechanism involved in making judgments in 
inductive reasoning
–
Reasoning based on observations
–
Reaching conclusions from evidence

pages.title: Inductive conclusions depend on the strength of the observations
pages.sourceText:
Inductive Reasoning
•
Inductive reasoning is the basis of scientific investigations
•
In science: observations are made, data are collected, and conclusions are drawn
–
In inductive reasoning conclusions we reach are probably, but not
definitely, true
•
Conclusions reached are suggested with various degrees of certainty
–
Strength of argument
•
Representativeness of observations
•
Number of observations
•
Quality of observations
Sometimes one very compelling high quality
observation can carry a lot of weight.

pages.title: Induction uses past experience to guide present behavior
pages.sourceText:
Inductive Reasoning
•
Used to make scientific discoveries
– Hypotheses and general conclusions
•
Used in everyday life
– Make a prediction about what will happen based on observation 
about what has happened in the past
– We make predictions and choices based on past experience, 
especially when predictions are based on familiar situations
• Provides a mechanism for using past experience to guide present behavior
– Some types of inductive reasoning happen automatically

pages.title: Heuristics are rapid rules of thumb that can produce errors
pages.sourceText:
Heuristics
•
When people use past experience to guide present behavior, they 
often use shortcuts to help them reach conclusions rapidly
•
“Rules of thumb” that are likely to provide the correct answer to a 
problem, but are not foolproof
•
Two more commonly used heuristics include the availability heuristic 
and the representativeness heuristic

pages.title: Availability substitutes ease of remembering for event probability
pages.sourceText:
•
Availability heuristic: events more easily remembered are judged as being 
more probable than those less easily remembered
•
Problem lies in factors that make events stand out in memory (e.g., 
distinctiveness, emotional salience, frequency of encoding / retrieval)
•
Availability is used to judge the probability of events
•
You use availability by trying to call to mind examples
•
The more examples you think of, the more probable you judge the 
event to be
Heuristics

pages.title: Words beginning with r are easier to retrieve than words with r third
pages.sourceText:
•
Which are more prevalent in English, words that being with the letter r or 
words in which r is the third letter?
•
70% respond that more words begin with r, even though in reality three 
times more words have r in the third position
Heuristics

pages.title: Memorable causes of death can seem more likely than common causes
pages.sourceText:
•
Some possible causes of death are listed below in pairs. Within each pair, 
which cause of death do you consider to be more likely for people in the 
United States? That is, if you randomly picked someone in the US, would 
that person be more likely to die next year from cause A or cause B?
•
This is due to availability of the causes.
–
E.g. when people die of botulism, it is front-pages news
–
Deaths from asthma go virtually unnoticed
Heuristics

pages.title: Representativeness can displace the base rate in the Robert problem
pages.sourceText:
Heuristics
•
Representativeness heuristic: people often make judgments based on 
how much one event resembles another event
– The probability that A is a member of class B can be determined 
by how well the properties of A resembles properties normally 
associated with class B
•
America has about 2.2M farms and 120k libraries
•
We randomly pick one male from the population of the US: That male, 
Robert, wears glasses, speaks quietly, and reads a lot. Is it more likely 
that Robert is a librarian or a farmer?
•
More S predict that Robert is a librarian
•
➔they ignore the base rate of farmers and librarians in the US

pages.title: The lawyer–engineer judgment changes when Jack is described
pages.sourceText:
Heuristics
•
Rule S follow:
– Use base rate information if it is all that is available
– Use descriptive information if available and disregard base rate 
information
•
In a group of 100 people, there are 70 lawyers and 30 engineers.
What is the chance that if we pick one person from the group at
random that the person will be an engineer?
•
➔S get this right
•
Jack is a 45-year-old man. He is married and has four children. He is 
generally conservative, careful, and ambitious. He shows no interest 
in political and social issues and spends most of his free time on his 
many hobbies, which include home carpentry, sailing, and 
mathematical puzzles.
•
➔S say Jack is an Engineer

pages.title: The Linda problem violates the conjunction rule
pages.sourceText:
Heuristics
•
Conjunction rule: probability of two events cannot be higher than the 
probability of the single constituents
•
Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken, and very bright. She majored 
in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned with issues of 
discrimination and social justice, and also participated in antinuclear 
demonstrations. Which of the following alternatives is more 
probable?
1.
Linda is a bank teller
2.
Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement
•
82% pick 2

pages.title: The hospital question requires considering how many births are sampled
pages.sourceText:
Heuristics
•
People also make errors in reasoning by ignoring the importance of 
the size of the sample on which observations are based
–
A certain town is served by two hospitals. In the larger hospital about 45 babies 
are born each day, and in the smaller hospital about 15 babies are born each 
day. As you know, about 50% of all babies are boys. However, the exact 
percentage varies from day to day. Sometimes it may be higher than 50%, 
sometimes lower. For a period of 1 year, each hospital recorded the days on 
which more than 60% of the babies born were boys. Which hospital do you 
think recorded more such days?
1.
The larger hospital
2.
The smaller hospital
3.
About the same?
–
S: 1 - 22% , 2 - 22%, 3 - 56%

pages.title: The smaller hospital has more days above 60 percent boys
pages.sourceText:
Heuristics
•
People also make errors in reasoning by ignoring the importance of 
the size of the sample on which observations are based
–
A certain town is served by two hospitals. In the larger hospital about 45 babies 
are born each day, and in the smaller hospital about 15 babies are born each 
day. As you know, about 50% of all babies are boys. However, the exact 
percentage varies from day to day. Sometimes it may be higher than 50%, 
sometimes lower. For a period of 1 year, each hospital recorded the days on 
which more than 60% of the babies born were boys. Which hospital do you 
think recorded more such days?
1.
The larger hospital
2.
The smaller hospital
3.
About the same?
–
S: 1 - 22% , 2 - 22%, 3 - 56%
–
➔correct answer is 2

pages.title: The law of large numbers connects sample size with representativeness
pages.sourceText:
Heuristics
•
Law of large numbers: the larger the number of individuals 
randomly drawn from a population, the more representative the 
resulting group will be of the entire population
–
People often assume that representativeness holds for small samples, and this 
results in errors in reasoning

pages.title: Illusory correlations can be reinforced by stereotype-consistent attention
pages.sourceText:
Heuristics
•
Illusory correlations: correlation appears to exist, but either does not 
exist or is much weaker than assumed
•
They can occur when we expect two things to be related, so we fool 
ourselves into thinking they are related even when they are not
– Stereotypes: Oversimplified generalizations about a group or class 
of people that often focuses on the negative
• A stereotype about a group may lead people to pay particular attention to 
behaviors associated with that stereotype
• This attention creates an illusory correlation that reinforces the stereotype
• Related to the availability heuristic because selective attention to the 
stereotypical behaviors makes these behaviors more “available”

pages.title: Lord and colleagues found belief-consistent evaluation of the same article
pages.sourceText:
Confirmation Bias
Lord and coworkers (1979)
•
Had those in favor of capital punishment and those against it read the same article
•
Those in favor found the article in favor
•
Those against found the article against
The “myside” bias: tendency for people to generate and evaluate evidence
and test their hypotheses in a way that is biased toward their own opinions
and attitudes
➔S focused on information that agreed with their beliefs and
disregarded information that didn’t

pages.title: Confirmation bias narrows the search in the 2, 4, 6 task

pages.title: Expected utility theory predicts choices with maximum expected benefit
pages.sourceText:
Decision-Making
•
Decision making: making judgments that involve choices between 
different courses of action
•
Utility: outcomes that are desirable because they are in the person’s 
best interest
•
Expected utility theory:
– People are rational
– If they have all relevant information, they will make a decision 
that results in the maximum expected utility
– Maximum monetary payoff

pages.title: Utility procedures do not fully describe what people choose
pages.sourceText:
Decision-Making
•
Advantages for utility approach
– Specific procedures to determine the “best choice”
•
Problems for utility approach
– Not necessarily money, people find value in other things
– Many decisions do not maximize the probability of the best 
outcome
• ➔people are not utility maximization machines
• e.g. people gamble in casinos all the time, even though they know that the 
odds are very much against them

pages.title: Avoiding air travel after September 11 increased exposure to road risk
pages.sourceText:
Decision-Making
•
After 9/11 a decrease in air travel and increase in driving occurred
– Even though the prob of dying in a car accident if far greater than 
in flying
– The number of Americans who lost their lives on the road to avoid 
flying is higher than the total number of passengers killed on the

pages.title: The convoy dilemma separates net lives saved from willingness to reroute
pages.sourceText:
An Example Dilemma
•
A convoy of food trucks is on its way to a refugee camp during a 
famine. (Airplanes cannot be used.) You find that a second camp 
has even more refugees. If you tell the convoy to go to the second 
camp instead of the first, you will save 1000 people from death, but 
100 people in the first camp will die as a result.
– Would you send the convoy to the second camp?
• U(notReRoute)=100-1000
• U(Reroute)=1000-100
– Ritov and Baron (1999): 63% did not choose to send the convoy 
to the second camp
• 12% responded that they would not change the route of the convoy 
even if only 1 person in the first camp would die

pages.title: Sacred values change responses to taboo and tragic tradeoffs
pages.sourceText:
Tetlock, Kristel, Elson, Green, Lerner (2000)
Sacred Value Protection Model
•
People want to protect what they hold sacred
– Sacred values are compartmentalized separately from secular values.
– When the two domains are intermingled, people feel threatened and 
they respond with moral outrage (Taboo).
– In contrast, when two sacred values are compared with each other, 
people are less morally outraged (Tragic).

pages.title: Saving Johnny competes with money in one scenario and another life in the other
pages.sourceText:
Tetlock, Kristel, Elson, Green, Lerner (2000)
•
Taboo Tradeoff Scenario
Robert can save the life of Johnny, a five year old who 
needs a liver transplant, but the transplant procedure 
will cost the hospital $1,000,000 that could be spent in 
other ways, such as purchasing better equipment and 
enhancing salaries to recruit talented doctors to the 
hospital. Johnny is very ill and has been on the waiting list 
for a transplant but because of the shortage of local 
organ donors, obtaining a liver will be expensive. Robert 
could save Johnny's life, or he could use the $1,000,000 
for other hospital needs.
•
Tragic Trade-off Scenario
There are two children who need a liver transplant, but 
only one liver.

pages.title: Ginges and colleagues examined tradeoff judgments among conflict-involved groups
pages.sourceText:
Ginges, Atran, Medin & Shikaki (2007)
•
Extended previous findings to a more realistic setting.
– Interviewed Israeli settlers (n=601), Palestinian refugees (n=535) and
Palestinian students who were affiliated with various political groups
(719)
•
Offered three types of tradeoff deals as possible solutions to the conflict.

pages.title: Material payment and symbolic recognition change the proposed deal differently
pages.sourceText:
Ginges, Atran, Medin & Shikaki (2007)
Taboo: Palestinians would recognize the sacred and historic right 
of the Jewish people to Israel. There would be two states: a 
Jewish state of Israel and a Palestinian state in 99% of the West 
Bank and Gaza.
Taboo+: On their part, Israel will pay Palestine 1 billion U.S. 
dollars a year for 10 years.
Symbolic: On their part, Israel will recognize the historic and 
legitimate right of the Palestinians to their own state and 
would apologize for all of the wrongs done to the Palestinian 
people.

pages.title: Moral absolutists reject compromise regardless of material benefit
pages.sourceText:
SV Measure
•
moral-absolutists: transformed the issues under dispute into sacred
values
– Among settlers: 46% of the sample
• believed that it was never permissible for the Jewish people to
‘‘give up’’ part of the ‘‘Land of Israel’’ no matter how great the
benefit.
– Among Palestinian students 54%
• treated both the principle of the ‘‘right of return’’ and Jerusalem
as sacred values.
•
non-absolutists: had strong preferences against compromise over these 
issues but did not regard them as sacred values

pages.title: Sacred-value negotiations can involve incentives as well as sanctions
pages.sourceText:
Sacred Values in Intergroup Conflicts
Investigate the impact of monetary incentives/disincentives in negotiations involving 
sacred values.
In two separate studies (Dehghani, Atran et al. 2010; Dehghani, Iliev et al. 2009):
•
How material incentives and disincentives, such as economic sanctions, 
psychologically affect the targeted population and potentially influence behavior
•
Investigated whether Iranians who treat the Iranian nuclear program as a sacred 
value would be amenable to material incentives/disincentives to compromise

pages.title: The Iranian study classifies sacred values through refusal of any consequence-based tradeoff
pages.sourceText:
Experiments
•
1997 Iranian participants in an online study conducted in Farsi
•
Dependent variables: people’s approval, people’s anger, misleading factor
•
The sacred value (SV) measure (based on Baron and Spranca’s 1997 measure): 
What do you think about Iran giving up its nuclear energy/weapons?
– a. I think this definitely needs to happen.
– b. I do not object to this.
– c. This should be done only if the benefits of stopping the program are great 
enough.
– d. This shouldn't be done no matter how great the consequences
•
Participants who answered ‘d’ were considered to have a SV (14% for nuclear 
energy, 13% nuclear weapons)

pages.title: The scenarios cross nuclear-program type with three kinds of deal
pages.sourceText:
Scenarios
•
2 (Nuclear program: nuclear energy vs nuclear weapons) * 3 (Type of deal: Taboo, 
Taboo+, Taboo-) design
•
Scenarios:
– Taboo: Iran will give up its program for developing nuclear energy(or weapons) and 
surrender the current nuclear facilities to the UN; in return Israel will give up their 
program for developing nuclear energy (or weapons) and surrender the existing nuclear 
facilities to the UN.
– Taboo+: taboo + In return, United Nations will give $40 billion dollars in economic 
funds to Iran.
– Taboo-: Taboo + You know that if Iran does not accept this deal, United Nations will 
impose additional sanctions on Iran.
•
Participants were asked:
–
Do you personally approve of this deal?
–
If the Iranian government approves such a deal do you think that people will be angry?
–
If such deal is really proposed to Iran do you find it misleading?
